paragraphs: An advertisement can promote an environmentally responsible image through its pictures and overall presentation, as well as its words. This paper introduces a benchmark for studying how oil and gas advertising frames its messages. The motivation is to make strategic communication easier to analyze at scale, including messaging that may contribute to greenwashing.

The dataset contains expert annotations of video advertisements from Facebook and YouTube. It covers 13 framing categories, more than 50 companies or advocacy groups, and 20 countries. Its emphasis on video makes it useful for evaluating vision-language models, extending beyond earlier datasets that treated framing primarily as a text analysis problem.

The reported results show uneven progress: GPT-4.1 achieves 79% F1 for environmental messages, while the best model reaches only 46% for green innovation framing. That gap highlights the difficulty of interpreting specific communication strategies. Implicit messages, varying video lengths, and cultural context remain stated challenges. The benchmark measures framing relevant to potential greenwashing; identifying an environmental message does not itself establish a mismatch between a company's claims and conduct.
neurips-2025-a-multimodal-benchmark-for-.tldr: This expert-annotated video benchmark tests how well vision-language models recognize oil and gas advertising frames relevant to potential greenwashing.

paragraphs: AdaDetectGPT addresses the problem of distinguishing human writing from text produced by a language model. Existing detectors often use statistics based on how probable a passage looks under a particular source model. The paper argues that relying solely on those log probabilities can leave useful detection performance unrealized.

The proposed classifier learns a witness function from training data. This function provides an adaptive way to distinguish the two kinds of text, enhancing detectors that use model probability information. The central idea is that the detection rule can learn from examples instead of depending exclusively on a fixed summary of how likely the observed passage appears.

The authors provide statistical guarantees for all four principal detection outcomes: correctly identifying generated text, incorrectly flagging human text, correctly identifying human text, and missing generated text. Numerical studies across combinations of datasets and language models show nearly uniform improvements over the compared state-of-the-art method, with improvements reaching 37%. The findings support adaptive detection in the evaluated settings while retaining the abstract's qualification that improvement is nearly, rather than completely, uniform.
neurips-2025-adadetectgpt-adaptive-detec.tldr: AdaDetectGPT learns an adaptive text detection function and provides statistical guarantees alongside nearly uniform empirical improvements over the compared leading method.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding speeds up language generation by having a small model propose tokens for a larger model to verify. Its effectiveness depends on how often those proposals are accepted. AdaSPEC starts from a mismatch in conventional training: making the small model imitate the larger model across every token does not directly optimize acceptance.

Because the draft model has limited capacity, trying to fit difficult tokens can interfere with learning the tokens it can model well. AdaSPEC uses a reference model to identify difficult-to-fit tokens and filters them out during knowledge distillation. This concentrates the draft model's training on simpler tokens where stronger alignment with the target is achievable.

The authors evaluate the method on arithmetic reasoning, instruction following, coding, and summarization, using two draft-and-target size combinations. AdaSPEC achieves higher acceptance rates than DistillSpec across all evaluated tasks, with reported improvements of up to 15%, without compromising generation quality. The practical contribution is a training objective better matched to the draft model's role: producing proposals that survive verification, rather than reproducing every aspect of the target's predictions.
neurips-2025-adaspec-selective-knowledge.tldr: AdaSPEC improves speculative decoding by filtering difficult tokens during draft-model distillation, increasing acceptance rates without compromising generation quality.

paragraphs: Finding unusual observations in scientific data involves two connected problems: extracting meaningful patterns from noisy, high-dimensional measurements and determining whether a deviation has statistical support. AutoSciDACT connects these steps in a general-purpose novelty detection pipeline. Its goal is to move beyond anomaly scores toward quantitatively supported comparisons with an expected reference distribution.

The pipeline first uses contrastive pretraining to produce compact representations of the data. This stage draws on high-quality simulations available in many scientific fields and on domain expertise for choosing principled data augmentations. The resulting embeddings make the data suitable for a sensitive machine-learning-based two-sample test using the New Physics Learning Machine framework.

That test compares observations with the reference distribution representing the null hypothesis, identifying and statistically quantifying deviations. Experiments span astronomical, physical, biological, image, and synthetic datasets, with strong sensitivity to small additions of anomalous data across those domains. The contribution is an initial unified route from representation learning to statistical testing, so that detecting novelty and assessing evidence for it are parts of the same workflow.
neurips-2025-autoscidact-automated-scien.tldr: AutoSciDACT combines contrastive representations with statistical two-sample testing to detect and quantify small deviations in scientific datasets.

paragraphs: Scene flow estimation describes motion in three-dimensional scenes. Using several frames can reveal temporal information that two-frame methods miss, but existing approaches can become much more expensive as additional frames are included. DeltaFlow is designed to use this extra temporal evidence without the rapidly increasing computation that motivates the paper.

Its lightweight 3D framework uses a delta scheme to extract temporal motion features at minimal computational cost regardless of frame count. The authors also address two learning problems. A category-balanced loss strengthens learning for underrepresented object classes, while an instance consistency loss encourages motion predictions belonging to the same object to remain coherent.

Evaluations on Argoverse 2, Waymo, and nuScenes report state-of-the-art performance. Compared with the next-best supervised multi-frame method, DeltaFlow achieves up to 22% lower error and twice as fast inference. The authors also report strong generalization across domains. These findings connect efficient temporal feature extraction with more accurate motion estimation, while the two additional losses target class imbalance and object-level inconsistency that temporal information alone does not resolve.
neurips-2025-deltaflow-an-efficient-mult.tldr: DeltaFlow combines inexpensive multi-frame motion features with balanced and consistent training losses to improve 3D scene flow accuracy and inference speed.

paragraphs: Unlearning aims to remove unwanted information or capabilities from a language model, but a few fine-tuning steps can undo current methods. The paper shows this vulnerability even when training imitates a model that never learned the unwanted information. Its explanation separates changed output behavior from underlying capabilities that can remain available inside the model.

The main finding is that training a randomly initialized student on an unlearned model's outputs transfers its behavior while leaving latent capabilities behind. Building on this result, the authors introduce UNDO, which distills an unlearned model into a noisy copy of itself. The amount of noise provides a tunable tradeoff between computational cost and resistance to relearning.

On synthetic language and arithmetic tasks, UNDO establishes an improved compute–robustness frontier. At its strongest setting, it matches retraining with perfectly filtered data while using 60–80% of the compute and labels for only 0.01% of pretraining data. The authors also report more robust unlearning on WMDP. These results support adding unlearning before distillation as a practical route to capability removal that better withstands subsequent fine-tuning.
neurips-2025-distillation-robustifies-un.tldr: Distilling an unlearned model can make capability removal more robust, and UNDO offers a tunable tradeoff between that robustness and compute.

paragraphs: Cooking combines movement, attention, and sequences of meaningful actions, making it a useful setting for studying complex human behavior. EPFL-Smart-Kitchen-30 captures people preparing recipes through synchronized measurements from several viewpoints and sensing modalities. The paper's central contribution is a dataset and benchmark suite for connecting visible actions with language and detailed human motion.

The recording platform uses nine fixed RGB-D cameras, inertial measurement units, and a head-mounted HoloLens 2. These capture external and first-person views alongside depth, eye gaze, and body and hand motion. The dataset spans 29.7 hours, 16 participants, and four recipes, with dense annotations averaging 33.78 action segments per minute.

Four benchmarks cover vision-language understanding, generating motion from semantic text, recognizing actions using multiple modalities, and segmenting actions from poses. Together, they support different questions about what a person is doing and how that activity unfolds physically. The authors present the resource as a foundation for improved behavior models and insights into naturalistic human activity, rather than reporting that those anticipated advances have already been achieved.
neurips-2025-epfl-smart-kitchen-an-ego-e.tldr: EPFL-Smart-Kitchen-30 provides synchronized video, gaze, and motion recordings of cooking, with four benchmarks for human behavior understanding and generation.

paragraphs: Einsum expresses computations that combine several input tensors into an output tensor. How those tensors are stored can strongly affect execution cost. Dense multidimensional arrays store the full structure, while coordinate lists provide a more compact representation when many entries are zero. The paper investigates why choosing one representation at the start can be inadequate.

The authors demonstrate a nontrivial example where coordinate lists are exponentially more efficient than arrays. They also emphasize the opposite practical possibility: coordinate lists can be substantially slower. The difficulty is that sparsity changes in intermediate tensors during computation, so the initial inputs do not make the best representation easy to predict.

Their solution switches from arrays to coordinate lists during execution according to the sparsity of the remaining tensors. This makes representation selection responsive to the computation as it unfolds. On established einsum benchmarks, the hybrid approach is consistently competitive with, or faster than, the better static representation. The finding supports adapting storage to evolving sparsity, without claiming that sparse storage is universally preferable.
neurips-2025-exploiting-dynamic-sparsity.tldr: A hybrid einsum evaluator adapts tensor storage to changing sparsity, matching or beating the better fixed representation in the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: Molecular dynamics follows atomic motion over time using interatomic forces. Machine learning can make force prediction cheaper, but conventional integration still needs very small time steps to handle rapid atomic motion. FlashMD targets this remaining obstacle by learning to predict how atomic positions and momenta evolve over substantially longer intervals.

The proposed strides are one to two orders of magnitude longer than typical molecular dynamics time steps. The architecture incorporates mathematical and physical considerations from Hamiltonian dynamics, tying the predictor to properties of the motion it models. The authors also generalize the approach to support any thermodynamic ensemble and examine possible failure modes of directly predicting molecular evolution.

Validation covers both equilibrium properties and properties that change over time, using models trained for particular systems as well as general-purpose models. The reported accuracy supports extending simulations toward longer time scales needed for scientifically and technologically relevant microscopic processes. The key contribution is therefore a longer advance through simulated time per prediction, complementing the existing strategy of reducing the cost of individual force calculations.
neurips-2025-flashmd-long-stride-univers.tldr: FlashMD predicts atomic positions and momenta over strides 10–100 times longer than typical molecular dynamics steps while reproducing evaluated equilibrium and time-dependent properties.

paragraphs: Event cameras provide asynchronous information with very fine temporal resolution, making them useful for perception in changing environments. However, detectors operating at a fixed frequency do not fully use that flexibility. FlexEvent addresses the problem of maintaining accurate object detection as the operating frequency changes, while combining event data with conventional RGB frames.

The framework has two complementary components. FlexFuse adaptively combines high-frequency events with the semantic information available in RGB images. FlexTune adapts fine-tuning to different frequencies by generating frequency-adjusted labels. Together, they address both the information being combined and the training supervision needed for the detector to generalize across operating rates.

Experiments on large event-camera datasets report improvements over state-of-the-art methods in standard and high-frequency settings. The method maintains robust performance when moving from 20 Hz to 90 Hz and produces accurate detections up to 180 Hz. The authors also report accuracy in fast-moving and static scenarios. These results support a more flexible detection system whose operating rate can vary without being restricted to one fixed-frequency training regime.
neurips-2025-flexevent-towards-flexible-.tldr: FlexEvent combines adaptive event–frame fusion with frequency-aware fine-tuning to support accurate object detection at varying rates, including up to 180 Hz.

paragraphs: FlowMixer forecasts patterns that evolve across both space and time using a single neural layer. Its design imposes mathematical structure on the computation to make learned dynamics easier to interpret. The model applies reversible transformations, mixes the transformed information through nonnegative matrices, and then applies the inverse transformations while preserving the data's shape.

This structure supports a Kronecker-Koopman eigenmode framework, which exposes interpretable patterns in the learned spatiotemporal dynamics. It also allows prediction horizons to be changed algebraically without retraining. A semigroup property means compositions of the layer can be represented within the same structured form, removing the need to search over depth for this architecture.

Experiments across several domains demonstrate long-horizon forecasting and modeling of physical behavior, including chaotic attractors and turbulent flows. The reported predictive performance matches state-of-the-art methods, with greater interpretability through directly extractable eigenmodes. The result suggests that carefully chosen architectural constraints can preserve forecasting quality while making the model's dynamics accessible to mathematical analysis and manipulation.
neurips-2025-flowmixer-a-depth-agnostic-.tldr: FlowMixer uses a mathematically structured single layer to deliver competitive long-horizon forecasts with interpretable dynamics and adjustable prediction horizons.

paragraphs: Recurrent models offer efficient processing of long sequences, but accessing a specific earlier part of the input is difficult. Adding attention can provide that access while threatening the original efficiency advantage. Hierarchical Sparse Attention, or HSA, is designed to give recurrent models selective access to distant context while preserving efficiency and length generalization.

HSA divides the input into chunks, selects the top relevant chunks, and aggregates their information hierarchically. Its selection mechanism learns relevance using fine-grained information from tokens inside each chunk. This aims to make chunk selection precise even when context lengths differ from training. A hardware-aligned kernel design supports efficient execution of the attention mechanism.

Combining HSA with Mamba produces RAMba. Despite pretraining on contexts of length 4K, RAMba reports perfect passkey retrieval at context lengths reaching 64 million, alongside improvements on several downstream tasks and a nearly constant memory footprint. The retrieval result demonstrates a striking tested case of length generalization; the broader downstream improvements support the usefulness of selective historical access beyond that particular task.
neurips-2025-hardware-aligned-hierarchic.tldr: HSA gives recurrent models efficient selective access to distant context, enabling RAMba's reported perfect passkey retrieval at lengths reaching 64 million.

paragraphs: Polymers consist of repeating structural units, so their graph descriptions can contain different numbers of repeats. A useful representation should remain consistent when this choice of description changes. The paper argues that existing graph neural network methods, which often model a single unit, fail to provide this consistency for the underlying polymer structure.

Graph Repetition Invariance, or GRIN, combines graph alignment based on a maximum spanning tree with augmentation using repeated units. The alignment and augmentation work together to preserve structural consistency across representations. The authors provide theoretical guarantees from both the model and data perspectives, identifying three repeating units as the minimal augmentation required for optimal invariant representation learning in their analysis.

On benchmarks covering homopolymers and copolymers, GRIN outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and produces stable representations that generalize to chains of unseen sizes. The practical significance is that changing the number of repeats used to describe a polymer need not change its learned identity. The theoretical result also supplies a specific augmentation requirement for the proposed approach.
neurips-2025-learning-repetition-invaria.tldr: GRIN learns polymer representations that remain stable across different repeat counts, with theoretical guarantees and improved results on polymer benchmarks.

paragraphs: A sequence model may solve a task on training-length inputs yet struggle when the same task involves longer sequences. This paper studies how to make that extension more reliable, particularly for algorithmic reasoning. It introduces a framework for deriving length generalization bounds under specified assumptions that can be checked, rather than relying only on asymptotic analysis.

The theory identifies auxiliary tasks linked to the structure of the main task. Within the framework, strong performance on these auxiliary tasks together with the primary task is sufficient to guarantee length generalization. This is a conditional result: the guarantee depends on the framework's assumptions and the required performance, rather than following from multitask training alone.

The authors turn that result into a training procedure that optimizes the main and auxiliary tasks jointly. Evaluations on challenging synthetic benchmarks, including sorting and reversal, show significant improvements on substantially longer sequences. The contribution connects a theoretical sufficient condition to a concrete training strategy, giving auxiliary tasks a principled role in learning behavior that extends beyond observed sequence lengths.
neurips-2025-length-generalization-via-a.tldr: Task-related auxiliary training improves length generalization, supported by guarantees that hold under the paper's specified, verifiable assumptions.

paragraphs: MindOmni addresses image generation tasks that require multimodal inputs and complex reasoning. The paper proposes a unified vision-language model that incorporates reasoning into generation through reinforcement learning. Its aim is to bring understanding and generation into the same system, including situations where producing the requested output requires more detailed reasoning.

Training proceeds in three phases. First, the authors design the unified model with a decoder-only diffusion module. Next, they use supervised fine-tuning on chain-of-thought instruction data. Finally, Reasoning Generation Policy Optimization, or RGPO, uses multimodal feedback to guide policy updates. This sequence combines an integrated architecture, explicit reasoning-oriented supervision, and feedback-driven refinement.

The reported experiments show that MindOmni outperforms existing models on both understanding and generation benchmarks. The authors also highlight fine-grained reasoning generation, especially under mathematical reasoning instructions. These findings support the combined training approach as a way to improve generation that depends on reasoning, while demonstrating gains across the two capabilities the architecture is intended to unify.
neurips-2025-mindomni-unleashing-reasoni.tldr: MindOmni combines reasoning supervision and multimodal reinforcement learning to improve unified visual understanding and generation.

paragraphs: Understanding where objects belong is only part of spatial intelligence; an agent also needs to turn that understanding into an executable plan. MineAnyBuild evaluates this step through architectural building tasks in Minecraft. It targets the gap between answering spatial questions and planning concrete actions from human instructions that can combine multiple modalities.

The benchmark contains 4,000 curated spatial planning tasks. Agents must generate building plans that can actually be executed, with evaluation covering spatial understanding, spatial reasoning, creativity, and spatial commonsense. The authors also propose a data collection approach based on player-generated content, providing a route to continually expanding the task collection.

An evaluation of existing multimodal language model agents reveals severe limitations in their spatial planning abilities, alongside substantial potential for improvement. The benchmark's contribution is to make executable planning central to spatial evaluation. It provides a setting where interpreting an instruction and arranging a structure must connect through a usable plan, allowing future work to assess progress beyond question-answering performance.
neurips-2025-mineanybuild-benchmarking-s.tldr: MineAnyBuild tests whether multimodal agents can turn human instructions into executable Minecraft building plans across 4,000 spatial planning tasks.

paragraphs: A broad scientific idea may lack the methodological and experimental details needed to act on it. MOOSE-Chem2 formalizes the task of turning coarse research directions into detailed, experimentally actionable hypotheses. It treats the many possible combinations of hypothesis details as an optimization problem and investigates how effectively language models can search that space.

The proposed method builds hypotheses hierarchically, progressively adding and integrating details until it reaches specific experimental configurations. The authors show that this process smooths the model's internal reward landscape and makes optimization more effective. The study also asks whether model-preferred hypotheses align better with reference hypotheses and how scoring by diverse or identical model ensembles compares with individual models.

Evaluation uses a new benchmark of expert-annotated, fine-grained hypotheses drawn from recent literature. The hierarchical approach consistently outperforms strong baselines on that benchmark. The stated result supports structured search for detailed hypotheses; the ensemble questions describe additional issues investigated, without the abstract specifying their individual answers. The work's emphasis is on improving hypothesis construction and selection through progressively refined details.
neurips-2025-moose-chem2-exploring-llm-l.tldr: MOOSE-Chem2 uses hierarchical search to develop detailed scientific hypotheses and outperforms strong baselines on an expert-annotated literature benchmark.

paragraphs: Giving a language model more computation during generation can improve reasoning, but checking candidate answers also consumes resources. This paper examines how often a verifier should be invoked. It treats verification frequency as a tunable decision, extending beyond the common choices of checking every generation step or only checking completed outputs.

Variable Granularity Search, or VG-Search, introduces a parameter controlling that frequency. The algorithm unifies beam search and Best-of-N sampling within a broader search framework. Experiments vary compute budgets, generator–verifier combinations, and task characteristics to study how the appropriate granularity changes with the setting.

The findings show that selecting granularity dynamically can improve computational efficiency and scaling behavior. Adaptive versions report accuracy gains of up to 3.1% over beam search and 3.6% over Best-of-N while reducing floating-point operations by more than 52%. The main implication is that verification timing is itself an optimization opportunity: allocating checks more effectively can improve the balance between reasoning quality and the computation spent obtaining it.
neurips-2025-rethinking-optimal-verifica.tldr: VG-Search adapts how frequently generated reasoning is verified, improving reported accuracy while reducing computation compared with beam search and Best-of-N.

paragraphs: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation explains a model's output by redistributing relevance backward through its layers to the input. The paper identifies a missing component in existing Transformer versions of this method: positional encoding. Ignoring position loses relevance associated with structural information and violates conservation, the accounting principle governing how relevance is redistributed.

The authors redefine the explanatory input space using position–token pairs. This lets an explanation account for both what a token is and where it occurs. They develop theoretically grounded propagation rules for Rotary, Learned, and Absolute positional encodings, bringing these architectural components into the relevance calculation instead of leaving their contributions unassigned.

Experiments include fine-tuned classifiers and zero-shot foundation models such as LLaMA 3, spanning vision and language explainability tasks. The proposed method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in those evaluations. The contribution is both conceptual and practical: positional information becomes an explicit part of what an explanation attributes, and the resulting attribution rules improve the reported quality of Transformer explanations.
neurips-2025-revisiting-lrp-positional-a.tldr: Position-aware relevance propagation accounts for positional encodings and improves Transformer explanations across evaluated vision and language tasks.

paragraphs: Language model agents can coordinate under assigned roles, but cooperation is harder when agents pursue their own interests without explicit coordination guidelines. Misaligned incentives can produce poor collective outcomes. Shapley-Coop addresses this problem with a workflow inspired by temporary collaborations such as employment and subcontracting, where contributions and compensation help organize cooperation.

The workflow combines structured negotiation with Shapley-inspired reasoning about each agent's marginal contribution. Those estimates support coordination during the task and redistribution of outcomes after it. A pricing mechanism connects individual incentives to cooperative behavior, aiming to recognize contributions fairly while preserving the agents' ability to act autonomously.

The authors evaluate Shapley-Coop in two multi-agent games and a software engineering simulation. Across these settings, it consistently improves collaboration and supports equitable redistribution that reflects individual contributions during execution. The findings suggest that credit assignment can serve as an active coordination mechanism, rather than merely a score applied afterward: anticipating how rewards will be divided helps self-interested agents organize their joint work.
neurips-2025-shapley-coop-credit-assignm.tldr: Shapley-Coop uses negotiation and contribution-based rewards to improve cooperation among self-interested language model agents.

paragraphs: Models of interatomic interactions often use rotation-equivariant networks, whose outputs transform consistently when a structure is rotated. Their Clebsch-Gordan tensor products are computationally expensive. Tensor Decomposition Networks replace these operations with low-rank decompositions, producing an approximately equivariant alternative designed to reduce this central computational cost.

For the CP decomposition, the authors prove a uniform bound on the induced equivariance error and show that the approach can approximate any equivariant bilinear map. They also share weights across tensor-product paths to reduce parameters without compromising equivariance through that sharing. The replacement layer reduces tensor-product complexity from O(L^6) to O(L^4), where L is the maximum angular degree.

The layers can replace tensor products in existing networks. Evaluation includes PubChemQCR, a newly curated molecular relaxation dataset with 105 million DFT-calculated snapshots, alongside OC20 and OC22. Results show competitive predictive performance with substantial computational speedups. The contribution pairs an efficient approximation with theoretical control of its rotational error, while providing a separate weight-sharing strategy for further parameter savings.
neurips-2025-tensor-decomposition-networ.tldr: Tensor Decomposition Networks accelerate interatomic models through low-rank tensor products with bounded rotational equivariance error and competitive empirical performance.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes how overparameterized two-layer networks with quadratic activations learn from synthetic data in high dimensions. It seeks precise descriptions of training and test error, rather than only broad qualitative statements about generalization. The setting includes L2 regularization, which penalizes model weights during empirical risk minimization.

The key step translates the neural-network learning problem into a convex matrix sensing problem with nuclear norm penalization. That translation reveals a low-rank structure in the learned feature maps as the source of capacity control. It also makes tools from matrix factorization and convex optimization relevant to understanding the network's best achievable solutions.

The analysis characterizes global minima and derives sharp asymptotic errors and precise generalization thresholds. In particular, it explains how the width of the target function governs learnability. These are results for the specified quadratic-network and synthetic-data setting. Their broader conceptual value is to connect neural learning with low-rank matrix recovery, showing how an apparently large model can have its effective capacity governed by a more structured representation.
neurips-2025-the-nuclear-route-sharp-asy.tldr: A convex matrix-sensing reformulation yields precise high-dimensional error and learnability results for regularized, overparameterized quadratic networks.

paragraphs: Graph embeddings turn network-structured data into representations that machine learning models can use. Many existing embeddings are high-dimensional and difficult to interpret or visualize. TopER aims to provide a compact alternative whose features have a clearer connection to graph structure, making the representations useful for both analysis and prediction.

Topological Evolution Rate draws on topological data analysis and simplifies an approach based on persistent homology. It calculates how graph substructures evolve, using their evolution rates to form low-dimensional embeddings. This gives the resulting representation a structural interpretation and supports intuitive visual exploration of graph datasets.

The authors evaluate TopER-based models on molecular, biological, and social network datasets, covering classification, clustering, and visualization. They report results that match or exceed state-of-the-art methods across these evaluations. The significance is that making embeddings compact and interpretable does not prevent competitive task performance in the tested settings. TopER therefore connects a representation suited to human inspection with one that remains useful for automated graph learning.
neurips-2025-toper-topological-embedding.tldr: TopER creates compact, interpretable graph embeddings from topological evolution rates while achieving competitive classification and clustering performance.

paragraphs: Uncertainty estimation in stream networks must account for locations connected by directional flow and dependencies that change over time. Predictions at these locations are interrelated, making joint uncertainty difficult to represent. The paper argues that existing conformal methods either overlook these dependencies and become overly conservative or fail to use the network's topological structure.

Spatio-Temporal Adaptive Conformal Inference, or STACI, incorporates both network structure and temporal dynamics. Its topology-aware nonconformity score measures prediction mismatch while respecting directional flow constraints. The framework also adjusts prediction sets dynamically as the data distribution shifts over time, connecting spatial structure with adaptation to changing conditions.

The authors provide theoretical validity guarantees and evaluate the method on synthetic and real-world datasets. STACI achieves a better balance between coverage and prediction efficiency than existing conformal approaches for stream networks. This balance matters because uncertainty sets should include the outcomes they are intended to cover without becoming unnecessarily broad. The reported results support using known network structure to make those sets more informative.
neurips-2025-topology-aware-conformal-pr.tldr: STACI incorporates directional network structure and temporal adaptation into conformal prediction to improve uncertainty sets for stream networks.

paragraphs: Membership inference tests try to determine whether a particular example appeared in a language model's training data. Exact-match definitions have proved difficult for existing tests, motivating a broader definition that also counts semantically similar examples as members. This paper asks whether that relaxation makes the tests reliable when the training data can be poisoned.

The authors show that poisoning can still cause a test to classify a chosen target incorrectly under the broader definition. Their theoretical analysis identifies a tradeoff between test accuracy and resistance to poisoning. They also construct a concrete attack, connecting the theoretical vulnerability to an experimentally evaluated way of manipulating training data.

Empirical results show that the attack can push existing tests to performance well below random. This is a claim about what the demonstrated poisoning can achieve, rather than a claim that every membership test always fails. The central implication is that broadening membership to include semantic neighbors does not resolve this reliability problem: accuracy and robustness to deliberate training-data manipulation remain distinct concerns.
neurips-2025-what-really-is-a-member-dis.tldr: Training-data poisoning can undermine membership inference even when membership includes semantic neighbors, exposing an accuracy–robustness tradeoff.
